lede: An IB Diploma with 24 points opens every programme in Denmark — if you also meet that programme's subject requirements.

deeper.label: How to apply, step by step

why.short: No tuition at all for EU, EEA and Swiss citizens, and SU on top if you hold Danish citizenship or, as another EU/EEA citizen, gain equal status (in practice through part-time work).

body.html:
• No tuition at all for EU, EEA and Swiss citizens, and SU on top if you hold Danish citizenship or, as another EU/EEA citizen, gain equal status (in practice through part-time work).
  • One application, one portal, one deadline, up to eight ranked choices.
  • The conversion from IB points to the Danish grade average is published, so you can work out where you stand before you apply.
  • You can apply before you have results — your IB coordinator sends them directly through the IB's results service.
  • Several strong English-taught programmes sit in cities far cheaper than Copenhagen.

watch.short: The deadline is 12:00 noon on 15 March, not midnight, and it applies to every IB holder including those who took the IB in Denmark.

body.html:
• The deadline is 12:00 noon on 15 March, not midnight, and it applies to every IB holder including those who took the IB in Denmark.
  • Most bachelor's degrees are taught in Danish and require Danish at A level or a pass in Studieprøven. The English-taught set is concentrated in a handful of institutions.
  • Universities must cut academic bachelor intake by roughly ten per cent across 2025–2029, so older cut-off figures understate how competitive some programmes now are.
  • If you can claim SU (Danish citizens, and EU/EEA citizens with equal status): the SU reform taking effect on 1 January 2027 cuts the grant frame for higher education from 70 to 58 portions and limits SU to the prescribed length of your programme.
  • Applicants without MitID must print the signature page, sign it by hand and send it to every institution by 15 March, 12:00. It is never uploaded, and the application is incomplete without it.

living.short: Danish universities have no tradition of campus accommodation.

body.html:
Residency

EU and EEA citizens apply to SIRI for an EU registration certificate within three months of arriving, bringing a passport and letter of admission. Then a CPR number from your municipality, then a health card, then a bank account and NemKonto — each step depends on the one before it. If you already live in Denmark and hold a CPR number, you have done this already.

Working

EU, EEA, Nordic and Swiss citizens can work without restriction. Others get a limited permit: 90 hours a month from September to May and full-time in June, July and August.

Housing

Danish universities have no tradition of campus accommodation. Most students live in kollegier, often some distance from campus, or rent privately. Start months before you arrive and contact your institution the moment you are accepted — August and September are the worst possible time to arrive without a room.

Healthcare

Once you have a CPR number you receive a health card automatically and healthcare is free. Choose insurance group 1, as 98% of residents do: an assigned GP, free consultations, referrals to specialists. Dental care and physiotherapy are not covered.

citizens.short: If you hold Danish citizenship, SU is yours without applying for equal status.

body.html: Your IB is converted to the Danish scale exactly as everyone else's is.

Sources

  1. Uddannelses- og Forskningsstyrelsen — checked 2026-09-24
  2. Eurydice — checked 2026-09-22

ib.short: The Agency converts your IB total to the Danish scale: 30 points is 6.9, 36 is 9.3, 40 is 10.7.

body.html:
The Agency publishes a conversion table each year. That average is what you compete on in quota 1.

The full table

subjects.short: HL generally becomes A level and SL becomes B — but not always, and the exceptions matter.

body.html:
Both mathematics courses — Analysis and Approaches and Applications and Interpretation — count the same way at each level. Global Politics has no fixed national equivalence; a few universities publish their own rule for it, and the programme pages show it.

Almost every programme names subjects and levels, and some name minimum grades too. Meeting the general entry requirement is not enough on its own.

Check yours against real programmes

apply.short: Apply by **15 March 2027, 12:00 noon CET**. IB candidate results: 6 July. Coordinated admission decisions: 28 July.

body.html:
That deadline applies to every applicant with an international qualification, including an IB taken at a Danish school, and whether you are aiming at quota 1 or quota 2. Your IB coordinator sends your results directly through the IB's results service — you do not wait and upload them yourself.

Step by step: how to apply

sources.title: IB candidate results for May sessions are available from 6 July; this is the examination-results step.
Applicants in Denmark’s coordinated admission system receive the admission decision on 28 July.

selection.short: Quota 1 ranks on your converted average alone; quota 2 weighs other things. You are considered for both.

body.html:
Programmes with more applicants than places split their intake into two quotas. Quota 1 takes most of the places. Quota 2 takes a smaller number and weighs whatever each institution publishes — typically grades in the required subjects, relevant work or study (Aalborg counts up to twelve months), and sometimes an admission test or an essay.

If you apply by 15 March and your average can be converted to the Danish scale, you are automatically considered in quota 1 as well as quota 2.

Aalborg's admissions office is unusually blunt about what does not count in its quota 2: motivational letters and recommendations are not considered relevant and are not required. Other institutions — Copenhagen Business School in particular — do want an essay. Check each one.

Fewer places than before

Denmark's universities must cut their bachelor intake by about ten per cent between 2025 and 2029 under the national dimensioning policy. Some programmes have fewer places than they did when older cut-off figures were published.

language.short: The English-taught set is much smaller.

body.html:
This is the single biggest constraint on studying in Denmark with an IB. The University of Copenhagen puts it plainly on its own bachelor page: 78 programmes, all taught in Danish. Aalborg has historically taught four in English. Most of the English-taught provision sits at Copenhagen Business School, Southern Denmark, the IT University, Roskilde and the university colleges.

If you took Danish A1 or Danish A Literature — at either level — you are fine. If you did not, and the programme is taught in Danish, you will need the Studieprøven language test or an equivalent.

The shape of Denmark's system

Denmark does not have one higher education sector but five, and they are genuinely different institutions rather than tiers of the same one. The Agency names them as universities, university colleges, business academies, institutions in architecture and art, and maritime educational institutions. Almost everything an IB student is told about Denmark concerns the first of those, which is a shame, because for some people the answer is one of the others. A reform is currently under way across the whole sector except maritime programmes, so structures that have been stable for years may not stay that way.

  • universitet

    university

    The eight research universities, and the route almost every IB student is shown. A three-year bachelor followed by a two-year kandidat (master’s), taught by people doing research in the subject. Academic in emphasis rather than vocational: you will read a great deal and write a great deal, and the first job comes after the master’s rather than after the bachelor.

    Open to IB Some English-taught

    The English-taught bachelor programmes listed on this site are almost all here. Most university bachelor programmes are still taught in Danish.

  • professionshøjskole

    university college

    Where Denmark trains nurses, teachers, social workers, midwives and a good deal of its engineering. The qualification is a professionsbachelor, typically three and a half to four years including a substantial paid or assessed placement, and it is designed to put you into the profession rather than into a master’s. If you already know you want to do the job rather than study the subject, this is the route that does that, and it is the one nobody mentions.

    Open to IB Rarely English-taught

    The overwhelming majority of professionsbachelor programmes are taught in Danish, which is the practical barrier rather than the entry requirements.

  • erhvervsakademi

    business academy

    Short, applied, two to two and a half years, leading to an erhvervsakademiuddannelse — an academy profession degree. Strongly vocational: multimedia design, computer science, marketing management, construction. Crucially it is not a dead end, because a one-to-one-and-a-half-year top-up converts it into a full professionsbachelor, so you can commit to two years rather than four and decide later.

    Open to IB Some English-taught

    Some business academies, particularly in Copenhagen, teach in English. This is the least-known route open to an IB student and the one worth checking if a four-year commitment at eighteen feels like too much.

  • institutioner inden for arkitektur og kunst

    institutions in architecture and art

    The architecture schools, design schools, art academies, conservatoires and the film school. Admission runs on portfolio or audition, and grades matter far less than at a university — this is the one part of the Danish system where the usual logic of this site inverts. Preparation means a body of work built over months, not a supplementary course.

    Partly open to IB Some English-taught

    Entry is competitive in a different way from grade cut-offs, and each school publishes its own brief. A general portfolio satisfies none of them well.

  • maritime uddannelsesinstitutioner

    maritime educational institutions

    Training for navigation, marine engineering and shipping, regulated separately from the rest of the sector and explicitly outside the current reform. A genuine route into a global industry that Denmark happens to be very good at, and one almost no IB student considers.

    Not yet checked Language of instruction not yet checked

    Not covered in detail on this site; the Agency names it as part of the sector. Ask the institutions directly.

money.short: Nothing for EU, EEA and Swiss citizens. Everyone else pays roughly €6,000–16,000 a year.

body.html:
Non-EU students also pay an application fee of roughly €100–200 to each university, and DKK 3,060 (2026 rate) for the residence permit.

If you hold a residence permit under Denmark's Special Act for displaced persons from Ukraine (Act no. 324 of 16 March 2022), you pay neither tuition nor the application fee.

SU is DKK 7,426 a month before tax in 2026 if you live away from your parents. Danish citizens can claim it, and so can EU/EEA citizens with equal status — through a parent who works in Denmark, five years living in Denmark or your own job. If you cannot claim SU, look first at your own country's student finance: several EU/EEA systems fund a full degree in another country.

Money, SU and the cost of living

context.short: Denmark teaches many master's degrees in English. At bachelor's level it mostly does not.

body.html:
Denmark is less English-taught than it looks

Denmark teaches many master's degrees in English. At bachelor's level it mostly does not. The University of Copenhagen — founded in 1479, with about 36,800 students — teaches all 78 of its bachelor programmes in Danish, and most Danish bachelor's degrees are the same. The English-taught bachelor's offering is real, and it is a specific and fairly narrow set of programmes rather than a choice you can make freely across the country. That is why this site lists the ones it does and not more: the list is short because the reality is.

Not to be confused with: This is not a rule about you. If you have Danish at A level, or take Studieprøven, the Danish-taught programmes are open to you and the choice becomes much wider.

The University of Copenhagen's own bachelor pages, read September 2026 Several sources agree on this

There is no single Danish quota 2

Quota 1 is national and mechanical: your converted grade average against a published cut-off. Quota 2 is not. The national agency's position is that quota 2 places are allocated "according to criteria published by the institution", which means each institution decides what counts and the criteria genuinely differ between them.

The practical consequence is that there is no general Danish quota 2 strategy to follow, and advice that describes one is describing a single institution. Aalborg states plainly that motivational letters and recommendations are not considered relevant to its quota 2 assessment. Copenhagen Business School requires a motivational essay. Southern Denmark uses an admissions test. Those are three different answers to the same question, all correct, at three universities in one small country.

Check the quota 2 page of the specific programme you want, and treat anything more general than that as background.

Not to be confused with: This is not the deadline, and not a suggestion that quota 2 is optional. Applying by 15 March at 12:00 puts you in both quotas automatically if your average converts.

The Danish Agency for Higher Education and Science, with the institutional examples read from each university's own pages Several sources agree on this

sections.html:
Denmark

How to apply, step by step

From choosing programmes in autumn 2026 to accepting a place in August 2027.

Christian Rasmussen from Copenhagen S, Denmark · CC BY-SA 2.0

  1. Home
  2. Denmark
  3. How to apply

  1. Autumn 2026 Work out what you qualify for

    Check your six subjects and levels against the programmes you want: autumn is when a missing subject can still be fixed. Check my subjects

    Ask for a pre-assessment

    Some universities will give you a written pre-assessment between September and December — ask.

  2. January–February 2027 Log in and gather documents

    Log in to optagelse.dk with MitID, or with your email address if you have no Danish CPR number.

    Which documents

    You will need your most recent transcript, documentation of anything you want counted in quota 2, and a passport copy if you are not an EU citizen.

  3. Before 15 March Ask your IB coordinator for the results service

    IB candidate results are available on 6 July, after the application deadline. Ask your coordinator to arrange official results delivery to each Danish institution.

    Institution codes

    Your coordinator registers you for the IB's own results service. Get a receipt. Institution codes: Copenhagen 002600, Aarhus 000150, Aalborg 000148, Southern Denmark 000157.

  4. 15 March 2027, 12:00 noon CET Submit up to eight programmes, and sign them

    List them in order of priority and sign every application by the same deadline. You get at most one offer: your highest-ranked programme that admits you.

    Signing, with or without MitID

    Order matters; think about it properly rather than ranking by prestige.

    With MitID you sign inside optagelse.dk. Without MitID you must print the signature page, sign it by hand and email or post it to every institution you apply to — it is never uploaded, and your application is not complete without it.

  5. Spring to 5 July Top up your documentation

    You can reorder your priorities until 12:00 on 5 July. Documentation deadlines are set by each institution.

    Each institution’s deadline

    Aarhus and Aalborg accept documents until 5 July, but Copenhagen wants them with the application on 15 March and some academies set 1 April. Check each one you list.

  6. 6 July IB candidate results

    If you registered for the results service, your results travel to the Danish institutions without you doing anything.

  7. 28 July Coordinated admission decisions

    Offers go out and every programme’s quota 1 cut-off is published. If you were not admitted anywhere, vacant places appear now.

  8. Early August Accept within a few days

    The deadline is the institution’s: in 2026, 2 August at Copenhagen, 3 August at Southern Denmark and 5 August at Aalborg.

    Then housing, CPR and a bank

    Then housing, CPR registration and a bank account — in that order, because each one depends on the last.

    The order you have to do things in

These dates beside any other country’s, on Deadlines

If you will pay tuition

The rules are harsher and differ by institution. At Aarhus you cannot apply in the year you take the IB, so check early: this can rule out the whole year.

Who this applies to

If you will pay tuition — you are not an EU, EEA or Swiss citizen and hold no permit that exempts you, such as permanent residence or a Special Act permit for displaced persons from Ukraine (see Money) — the rules are harsher and differ between institutions. Aarhus says that "if you are a paying applicant, then you cannot apply if you earn your IB exam in the year of application", because paying applicants must document everything by 15 March. Aalborg sets 1 May. Check your specific institution early, because this can rule out the whole year. If you do not pay tuition, these harsher rules do not apply to you.

If you are a subject short

Top up the missing level through GSK. It is taught in Danish, and only meets a specific subject requirement.

How GSK works

Denmark lets you top up through GSK (gymnasial supplering) — individual subjects taken at a VUC or GSK centre to reach a level you are missing. Two things to know: GSK subjects are taught in Danish, and GSK cannot be used to raise your overall qualification level, only to meet a specific subject requirement.

The separate rules about supplering — two successive level raises, at least one to A level — apply only if you hold DP Course Results rather than a full Diploma (what qualifies you).

Taking a sabbatår

A year out carries no penalty in quota 1, and relevant work can help in quota 2.

Why it costs nothing

Taking a year out after the IB is ordinary in Denmark and carries no penalty in quota 1 — your average is your average. The old bonus for applying within two years of finishing no longer exists. A year of relevant work can genuinely help in quota 2, where many institutions count documented work — Aalborg up to twelve months.

Portal

optagelse.dk

Deadline

15 March 2027, 12:00 CET

Max programmes

8, ranked

Offers

28 July 2027

Documentation

Set by each institution — 15 March to 5 July

On ranking

Rank your eight choices by where you would actually rather be, not by how hard they are to get into. You only ever receive one offer — the highest-ranked programme that accepts you — so a long-shot at number one costs you nothing.

sections.html:
Denmark · Official rules

How Denmark converts your IB

The official tables, from the Agency's Eksamenshåndbogen — not the out-of-date summaries some universities publish.

Finn Årup Nielsen · CC BY-SA 4.0

  1. Home
  2. Denmark
  3. Conversion

Your IB total as a Danish average

Enter your predicted total, including the three bonus points for Theory of Knowledge and the Extended Essay.

Statistisk omregning 2026, Uddannelses- og Forskningsstyrelsen. The table for the summer 2027 intake is published by 1 March 2027, and may move these figures by a decimal or two.

What a Danish requirement means in IB terms

Danish A, B and C are levels of study, not grades. A is the highest, and a higher level always covers a lower one.

Every requirement a programme here asks for ({{requirementCount}})

Danish A, B and C are levels of study, not grades. A is the highest level a subject can be taken at and C the lowest, and a higher level always covers a lower one. So when a programme asks for English B, it means English at B level — not the IB course English B, although English B SL is one way to meet it. Any IB English means any English A or English B course — not English ab initio.

Every subject a programme on this site asks for, read through the Agency's handbook. SL or HL means either level meets it. Where a university publishes its own additions, they are named under the national answer.

{{requirements}}

A minimum grade is converted with the single-grade table: the lowest IB grade that converts to the Danish minimum or above. The handbook's full subject table is under subjects and levels.

Total points to Danish grade average

The number you compete on in quota 1. There is no bonus on top of it, and it is re-issued every year.

The table, 18 to 45 points

This is the number you compete on in quota 1. It is re-issued every year — the table below is labelled Statistisk omregning 2026, Uddannelses- og Forskningsstyrelsen, and the version for the summer 2027 intake is published by 1 March 2027.

There is no bonus on top of it. The admission order in force for universities (Adgangsbekendtgørelsen, BEK nr 288 of 17 February 2026, § 17) ranks quota 1 on the exam average — for an IB Diploma, the converted average in this table — and contains no multiplier for applying soon after school. So a programme's cut-off and your converted average compare directly, and the IB points shown beside a cut-off on this site are read straight off this table. The same § 17 converts an exam only if it is from an EU or EEA country. § 18 puts applicants whose exam is from outside the EU/EEA in quota 2 only. An IB Diploma taken at a school in Denmark is converted like this.

{{average}}

If you finish in May 2027

  • The grade-average conversion table is re-issued every year. The table for a given summer intake is published by 1 March of that year and applies until the end of February the following year. If you are applying for August 2027, check for the table published by 1 March 2027 — the numbers below are the version current as of September 2026 and may shift by a decimal or two.
  • The single-grade table (used only where a programme sets a minimum grade in a subject) has been stable for years and is far less likely to move.
  • Subject-level equivalences change rarely. The current table already covers the post-2019 IB mathematics courses.

Single subject grades

Used only where a programme sets a minimum grade in a named subject. Never used to build your average.

IB grade 1–7 to the Danish scale

Used only where a programme sets a minimum grade in a named subject — Aalborg's Mathematics A at 4.0, or Copenhagen Business School's English B at 6.0. It is never used to build your average.

{{single}}

Where a subject was completed at several levels, the highest grade at or above the required level is used. A grade at a level below the one required does not count at all.

Subjects and levels: the handbook in full

39 Danish subject levels and the IB courses that meet each, plus the rule for other languages.

The full table

Prepared by the Danish Ministry of Children and Education. Danish levels are A (highest), B and C — they are levels of study, not grades.

{{subjects}}

Other languages

{{language.westernEuropean}}
{{language.other}}

The awkward cases

Global Politics, Theory of Knowledge, Danish ab initio and Geoscience A: no straightforward equivalent, and what to do about it.

All 4
Global Politics — No fixed national equivalence. Some universities publish their own rule.

Global Politics is 150 hours at SL and 240 at HL. Danish Social Studies (samfundsfag) B covers sociology, economics, politics and method; A adds international politics. Global Politics goes far deeper into international politics than Danish Social Studies A, but does not cover the sociology and economics that the Danish subject includes. Institutions decide case by case whether it meets Social Studies C, B or A — sometimes only in combination with another social science subject.

What to do

Aarhus publishes that Global Politics HL counts as Social Studies B, and Global Politics SL together with Economics SL or HL; CBS lists Global Politics at SL or HL for Social Studies B. The programme pages on this site show those routes where they apply. Anywhere else, write to the admissions office before 15 March and ask for a written assessment — do not assume it counts.

Theory of Knowledge (TOK) — No Danish equivalent.

TOK does not correspond to any subject in the Danish upper secondary system. Depending on what you covered, it may earn credit towards small parts of certain Danish subjects, but it does not satisfy a subject requirement.

Danish ab initio — Equivalent to nothing in the Danish-as-a-second-language ladder.

Danish ab initio, Danish B HL and Danish B SL are foreign-language subjects aimed at listening, speaking, reading and writing Danish. Whether Danish ab initio or Danish B HL can replace Danish A as the Danish-language requirement is left to each institution.

Geoscience A (Geovidenskab A) — No IB equivalent listed.

The handbook explicitly leaves the IB column blank for Geoscience A. IB Geography HL is not automatically accepted; the agency publishes a separate note comparing the two.

What qualifies you

  • An IB Diploma with 24 points or more: every programme, if you also meet its subject requirements.

  • DP Course Results, 18 points or more, every grade 3 or above, three at HL: academy profession and professional bachelor programmes. A university bachelor also needs two subject-level raises.

  • A retake: Denmark converts your original result, not the improved one.

Every case, and the retake rule
{{access}}

Retakes

Check the letter at the bottom left of your diploma. D is an original result, R is a retake. If you retook to improve a result that already qualified you, Denmark converts your ORIGINAL result, not the improved one.

Results timing

IB results are released on 6 July. Danish applications close on 15 March, so you apply before you have your results and ask your IB coordinator to send them directly through the IB's results service (up to six institutions).

Danish language

Most Danish bachelor programmes are taught in Danish, and for those you must document Danish at A level.

The four ways to meet it
  • Danish A1 HL / Danish A Literature HL — meets Danish A.
  • Danish A1 SL / Danish A Literature SL — normally accepted for Danish A at university, because it sits above the Studieprøven test.
  • Studieprøven i dansk — the national Danish language test for higher education. Universities may allow it in place of Danish A for applicants with a non-Nordic qualification.
  • Danish B HL or Danish ab initio — decided institution by institution. Ask in writing.

Studieprøven is not an upper-secondary subject, so it can never be used to meet a subject grade requirement — only the language requirement.

Sources

4 official sources, as of 2026-09-22.

Show them
  1. Eksamenshåndbogen — International Baccalaureate (Eksaminer, Fagniveauer, Karakterer) — checked 2026-09-22. Select 'International Baccalaureate' in the country/examination dropdown. Danish only.
  2. Optagelse af IB-elever og supplering af Diploma Programme (DP) Course Results — checked 2026-09-22
  3. Karakteromregning — general rules for converting foreign grades — checked 2026-09-22
  4. Vurdering af fagniveauer — Danish subject levels and teaching hours — checked 2026-09-22
Checked 22 September 2026

Worth knowing

A full IB Diploma does not require a grade of 3 in every subject. A 2 may appear, as long as the IB's own conditions for awarding the Diploma were met. Several Danish university pages say otherwise; the Agency's handbook is the governing source.

sections.html:
Denmark

Money, SU and what it actually costs

Tuition is free for EU, EEA and Swiss citizens. Everything else is not.

Karen Mardahl · CC BY-SA 2.0

  1. Home
  2. Denmark
  3. Money

What it costs

Indicative: Study in Denmark attaches no year to the tuition range or the budget, so ask the institution.
What, and who pays itAmount
TuitionEU, EEA and Swiss citizens; permanent residence or a permit that can lead to it; a Special Act permit (Ukraine)

None

TuitionEveryone else

≈ €6,000–16,000 a year

Application feeNon-EU/EEA applicants, at most universities (not Special Act permit holders)

≈ €100–200 per institution, by 15 March

Residence permitNon-EU students

DKK 3,060 (2026)

Living costsEveryone; more in Copenhagen

DKK 8,450–13,700 a month

SU, the state grantDanish citizens, and EU/EEA citizens with equal status

Up to DKK 7,426 a month (2026), before tax, for a student in higher education living away from their parents; plus a loan of up to DKK 3,799

SU: who can claim it

If you hold Danish citizenship, apply through minSU with MitID. Other EU, EEA and Swiss citizens are not automatically entitled: you apply for equal status, through one of three routes. If you moved to Denmark with your family, the first two usually fit.

A parent who works in Denmark

If you are the child of an EU/EEA citizen who works or is self-employed in Denmark, and you moved to Denmark before 21, you can apply for equal status. The right comes from your parent's work: it lasts while they keep that status, and stays with you while you remain in Denmark even if they leave.

Five years living in Denmark

An EU, EEA or Swiss citizen who has lived in Denmark continuously for at least five years, with the right of permanent residence, can apply for equal status. Absences of up to six months a year do not break it.

Your own job

Working at least 10–12 hours a week for a continuous period of at least 10 weeks gives worker status, and you have to keep working throughout the period you receive SU.

The Agency warns that working exactly 40 hours a month is usually not enough for the job route, because most months run longer than four weeks.

Non-EU students on a study residence permit are not allowed to claim SU or housing benefit, and doing so can cost them the permit.

Equal status under EU rules covers SU in Denmark and abroad. Equal status under Denmark's own rules — for example having come to Denmark with your parents — covers SU in Denmark only.

The 2027 SU reform affects this cohort

From 1 January 2027 the grant is limited to the prescribed duration of the programme, and the total frame drops from 70 to 58 portions.

What changes

An SU reform takes effect on 1 January 2027 and applies to anyone starting a new higher education programme on or after 1 July 2025 — which includes this cohort. The total grant frame for higher education drops from 70 to 58 portions, and SU is limited to the prescribed duration of your programme, with a completion loan of up to 24 months if you run out. Plan on finishing on time.

Taking SU to a degree abroad

SU can be taken to a full degree abroad by Danish citizens and by EU/EEA citizens with equal status under EU rules, if the programme is SU-approved and you also meet the ties-to-Denmark requirement. Citizenship alone is not enough.

The ties requirement, and for how long

You meet the ties-to-Denmark requirement through one of seven ties — for example two years of continuous residence in Denmark in the last ten, having gone to school in Denmark for a substantial period, or a parent who has worked in Denmark for five years. In another Nordic country SU is paid as if you studied in Denmark; elsewhere it is capped at four years (48 klip). Either way it uses SU klip, within an overall frame of 70 klip for higher education abroad. su.dk does not yet say how the 2027 reform changes that frame, so check there before counting on it.

If you cannot claim SU, look first at your own country's student finance: several EU/EEA systems fund a full degree in another country.

Tuition and fees

Free for EU, EEA and Swiss citizens and some permit holders. Everyone else pays roughly €6,000–16,000 a year, and an application fee.

Who is exempt, and the fees

Danish higher education is free for citizens of the EU, the EEA and Switzerland, and for anyone holding permanent residence or a temporary permit that can lead to it. If you hold a residence permit under the Special Act for displaced persons from Ukraine (Act no. 324 of 16 March 2022), you are exempt too, from both tuition and the application fee. Everyone else pays. Study in Denmark quotes a range of roughly €6,000–16,000 per year — about DKK 45,000–120,000 — but no year is attached to that figure, so treat it as indicative and ask the institution.

optagelse.dk charges nothing, but most universities charge non-EU/EEA applicants an application fee of roughly €100–200 per institution, payable by 15 March — Aalborg €150, Roskilde €200. An unpaid fee stops the application. Non-EU students then pay DKK 3,060 (2026 rate) for the residence permit itself.

Cost of living

Study in Denmark budgets DKK 8,450–13,700 a month. Its rent figure is optimistic in Copenhagen.

Housing

No campus tradition: most students live in kollegier or rent privately. Start months before you arrive.

Where to look

Danish universities have no tradition of campus accommodation. Most students live in kollegier — halls of residence, often some distance from campus — or rent privately. Start months before you arrive, and contact your institution about housing the moment you are accepted. August and September are the worst possible time to turn up without a room.

Where to look: ungdomsboliger.dk and studenterguiden.dk nationally; Kollegiernes Kontor in Copenhagen; Student Housing Aarhus; Studiebolig Aalborg; Boligoen and Kollegieboligselskabet in Odense.

Working while you study

EU, EEA, Nordic and Swiss citizens can work without restriction. Other students: 90 hours a month, September to May.

The hours, and SU through a job

EU, EEA, Nordic and Swiss citizens can work without restriction. Students from outside that group get a limited work permit: 90 hours a month from September to May, and full-time through June, July and August. Study in Denmark's own pages still quote the old 20-hours-a-week rule — the immigration service's 90 hours a month is the current one.

Students in Denmark typically work 10–20 hours a week. If you are an EU/EEA citizen without Danish citizenship and no other route to equal status, that job can also be your route to SU.

The order you have to do things in

Residence document, then CPR number, health card, and a bank account as your NemKonto: each needs the one before.

Each step

  1. Residence document

    If you are a Nordic citizen you need none: you register directly for a CPR number at Citizen Service. If you already live in Denmark as another EU/EEA citizen, you will usually have a registration certificate; ask SIRI whether yours needs updating once you are here as a student rather than as a family member. If you are arriving, EU and EEA citizens get an EU registration certificate from SIRI within three months. Book the appointment in advance and bring your passport and letter of admission. Non-EU students need a residence permit before arrival — allow two to three months.

  2. CPR number

    Your Danish personal number. If you already live in Denmark you have one, and it stays yours when you move for university — register the new address within five days. Otherwise your municipality issues it once you have an address and the right to stay.

  3. Health card

    Arrives automatically with your CPR registration. Choose insurance group 1 — 98% of residents do — which gives you an assigned GP with free consultations and referrals.

  4. Bank account and NemKonto

    Needs the CPR number. Register the account as your NemKonto so public bodies, including SU, can pay you.

Bring enough money for the first few weeks: rent plus a deposit will land before any of this is finished.

On that rent figure

Rent of DKK 3,000 a month appears in the official budget. In Copenhagen today that is optimistic. Aarhus, Odense, Aalborg, Esbjerg and Sønderborg are all materially cheaper, and several strong English-taught programmes are in exactly those cities.
